title: Microbatch coordinator: preemptive scheduling + python-shim prototype notes
content:
Context and motivation:

We keep seeing intermittent p95/p99 tail spikes for small-text generation requests (payloads < 256 bytes). These spikes are disproportionate to token compute on the GPU and correlate with CPU-side work during request ingress: JSON/header parse, UTF-8/unicode scanning in the tokenizer, and occasional Python GC/GIL pauses when the coordinator moves jobs between queues. This doc collects a focused set of experiments on two ideas that together reduced CPU tail contributions in our lab cluster: (1) a preemptive microbatch coordinator that avoids long blocking in the network/parse thread, and (2) a small native shim to move the hot unicode scanning path out of interpreted Python.

Observed symptoms (prod-like testbed):
- Workload: 2000 QPS of small generation requests (avg tokens requested: 16, prompt size < 200 chars), 64-concurrency client mix.
- Baseline p50/p95/p99 server-side latency (end-to-end, host-side only): 6 ms / 48 ms / 128 ms.
- Sampling profiler (py-spy, 10k stacks): tokenizer functions + json.loads accounted for ~42% of CPU samples during spikes.
- eBPF syscall traces showed bursts of futex/wake when coordinator moved items across queues.
- Perf/flamegraphs show long Python frames (~3–8 ms) where GIL is held while scanning bytes for token boundaries; content with emojis/2-byte codepoints amplified cost.

Hypothesis:
1) Coordinator design currently drains an internal queue with blocking calls that occasionally starve the network/parse worker — causing request-parse latency to spike. Preemptive scheduling (allowing the coordinator to yield during long microbatch assembly) should cap worst-case parse-to-dispatch time.
2) UTF-8/unicode scanning in pure-Python tokenizer is hot and causes significant GIL time. Moving the scanning loop into a narrow native shim (C/Rust) will reduce GIL hold time and lower p99.

Experiment 1: Preemptive microbatch coordinator behavior
- Change: coordinator loop was modified to assemble microbatches but break assembly if wall-clock assembly time exceeded 700us, then re-enqueue remainder (cooperative preemption). Also added a small fast-path: if in low-latency mode (requests-per-second < threshold), force single-request batching.
- Instrumentation: per-request timestamps at ingress, after parse, after batch assembly, and at GPU dispatch. Added counters: batch_assembly_time_ms, assembly_yields, net_requeued_count.
- Findings:
  - Assembly yield rate increased under bursty arrival patterns from 0 -> 3.2% of batches.
  - Mean batch_assembly_time dropped from 1.8ms to 0.9ms (measured on a 16-core worker).
  - p95 host latency reduced from 48ms to 33ms; p99 reduced from 128ms to 95ms in these runs.
  - Tradeoff: slightly increased GPU scheduling overhead (more but smaller batches), throughput unchanged for stable loads but higher variance in per-batch throughput.
- Notes: heuristic thresholds need calibration per instance size; added gauge to track increased GPU call rate to ensure no overload.

Experiment 2: Native shim for unicode scanning (pyshim prototype)
- Goal: keep tokenizer API in Python but move the tight scanning loop that computes token boundaries / codepoint classification into a native extension. Implemented a minimal CPython C-extension (50 LOC) which exposes: scan_token_boundaries(bytes) -> list[int] (offsets). Rust alternative using PyO3 was also prototyped but we used C-extension for fastest iteration.
- Microbench harness: generated synthetic prompts with different char classes: ascii-only, mixed-latin with accents, emoji-heavy, and CJK. Measured tokenization CPU time via perf and py-spy sampling.
- Results (relative to pure-Python tokenizer):
  - ascii-only: tokenization median reduced 0.6ms -> 0.25ms (~58% lower). p99 4.8ms -> 2.1ms.
  - emoji-heavy: median 1.3ms -> 0.4ms (~69% lower). p99 7.5ms -> 3.0ms.
  - CJK (multi-byte continuous): median 0.9ms -> 0.35ms. p99 6.2ms -> 2.6ms.
- End-to-end effect combined with preemptive coordinator: p99 host latency improved from baseline 128ms -> 64ms in the lab workload (approx 50% reduction).
- Observations:
  - GIL hold time reduced because native code does the tight loop and releases GIL (we used Py_BEGIN_ALLOW_THREADS in the C shim). CPU samples show much smaller Python frame stacks during tokenization phase.
  - However, allocations: native shim returned Python lists of integers which added conversion cost. We tried two variants: returning a packed bytes offsets array (memoryview) vs list[int]; memoryview cut conversion overhead by ~30%.
  - For very small payloads the conversion overhead becomes a non-negligible fraction; we use an in-place decode+callback to avoid materializing full offset arrays in the next iteration.

Profiling notes and commands used
- Data capture:
  - py-spy record -o flame.svg --pid <worker_pid> --native
  - sudo perf record -g -p <pid> -F 99 -- sleep 30
  - tcpdump -w parse-trace.pcap -s 0 port 443 and postprocess to correlate arrival timestamps.
- Microbench: wrk2 -t64 -c64 -d120s -R2000 --lua ./small-gen.lua http://localhost:8080/generate
- Harness: python tools/lab/microbatch_harness.py --load pattern=bursty --payload-set=emoji,ascii,cjk

Risks and caveats
- Native shim increases code surface and requires compiled artifact for each deployment target (we need to publish wheels / musl builds for private deployments). CI packaging needed.
- Returning large Python objects from native code can negate wins; prefer memoryviews or iterator callbacks.
- Releasing GIL is necessary; if native code calls back into Python for token post-processing we re-introduce GIL waits.
- Preemptive yielding increases the number of GPU invocations and may harm throughput on highly steady high-volume workloads; we need an adaptive policy that accounts for both latency SLO and cost per-token.

Next steps / proposed plan
1) Convert the shim prototype to a small Rust extension (PyO3) and upstream CI build for our supported platforms (x86_64 linux, arm64). This will make future micro-optimizations easier and reduce memory-safety risk.
2) Implement a secondary fast-path that returns offsets as a packed bytes buffer + length metadata to avoid Python list allocation. Add an API to let the serving runtime consume the offsets without creating intermediate Python objects.
3) Extend coordinator preemption: make thresholds adaptive based on observed arrival liveness and target SLO (e.g., keep percentiles inside SLO while limiting batch count growth).
4) Canary: deploy to a single dedicated capacity node with telemetry enabled (batch_size_distribution, assembly_yield_rate, tokenization_native_time, tokenization_python_time). Run 24h soak with production traffic replay.
5) If safe, roll out to dedicated pools with an opt-in toggle for private customers; for hosted API include as part of a rollout experiment with A/B.

Open questions for the team
- Packaging strategy for native extensions: wheels vs multi-arch static builds in runtime image? (ops preference?)
- Do we want the coordinator to expose a backpressure metric to clients when we detect too many small batches? Alternative: server-side adaptive token insertion heuristics.
- Is there appetite to move more of the parsing stack into native code (headers, JSON parsing) vs optimizing the Python call patterns?

Appendix: quick code sketch (conceptual)
- C shim sketch: uses PyArg_Parse to get bytes, Py_BEGIN_ALLOW_THREADS, scan bytes for utf-8 continuation/leading bytes to compute offsets, write offsets into a pre-allocated PyBytes object, return memoryview.
- Coordinator pseudo: while running: start = now(); while assembly_time < budget && items < max_batch: pop; assemble; if now()-start > budget: push remainder; break; dispatch(batch);

Summary
Moving the tight unicode/token-boundary scan into native code and making the microbatch coordinator preemptive produced the largest single-host p99 reductions we've seen for tiny requests. The prototype shows a clear direction: narrow native shims + adaptive preemption. Packaging and careful conversion-free APIs are the main engineering work left before a safe canary.

Notes log: 2024-11-05 initial prototype; 2024-11-08 memoryview conversion optimization; 2024-11-12 combined run with preemption heuristics.
